name: Skin booster injectables (Profhilo)

lead: Skin boosters are injectable hyaluronic acid products intended to improve hydration and elasticity rather than to add volume. Profhilo, made by IBSA Derma and launched in 2015, is the best-known example and is discussed for crepey or thin skin, including around the eyes.
Published support is described as mostly small open-label studies, some with manufacturer involvement.

paras: Profhilo is described as a 2 ml syringe of 64 mg non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid, half high- and half low-molecular-weight, said to stimulate collagen and elastin.

Reported effects are mostly mild injection-site reactions such as swelling, redness, bruising, pain and itching, usually resolving within a day or two. Contraindications listed include hyaluronic acid hypersensitivity, bleeding disorders and active skin infection.

lead: Skin boosters, or injectable moisturizers, are hyaluronic acid (HA) preparations injected into the skin to improve hydration and quality rather than to fill volume. Profhilo, produced by IBSA Derma, a unit of the Swiss IBSA group, is the best-known brand and was launched in 2015.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source that cites partly manufacturer and clinic material, describes the evidence as mostly small open-label studies from 2015 to 2022 and notes no independent randomized trials were cited.[1] Hyaluronic acid itself is abundant in skin and helps keep tissue hydrated.[2]
infobox: Not FDA-approved as of January 2026, per Grokipedia

paras: Profhilo is described as a 2 ml syringe containing 64 mg of non-cross-linked HA, split between high- and low-molecular-weight forms, using the maker's NAHYCO technology.[1] It is intended to address skin firmness and laxity rather than add volume.[1]

Claimed benefits include hydration, elasticity and reduced laxity lasting about four to six months, with a standard protocol of two sessions about a month apart.[1] Reported figures include a roughly 29 percent rise in hydration and a 21 percent reduction in neck laxity.[1]
Side effects are mostly mild and short-lived injection-site reactions.[1] HA fillers generally can cause erythema, itching and, rarely, vascular occlusion.[2]

Studies are described as small, open-label and partly manufacturer-funded, with 11 to 64 participants, and a postmarketing figure of over 42,000 patients.[1] No studies specific to the under-eye area were found.

timeline.event: Profhilo launched and CE-marked in Europe.[1]
